questions.question_text:
Which one of the following sequences when stored in an array at locations
A[1], . . . , A[10] forms a max-heap?
questions.subtopic: Trees, binary search trees, binary heaps
questions.explaination: In a 1-indexed max-heap, every node at index $i$ must satisfy $A[i] \ge A[2i]$ and $A[i] \ge A[2i+1]$. For sequence B $[23, 17, 14, 7, 13, 10, 1, 5, 6, 12]$: $A[1]=23 \ge A[2]=17, A[3]=14$; $A[2]=17 \ge A[4]=7, A[5]=13$; $A[3]=14 \ge A[6]=10, A[7]=1$; $A[4]=7 \ge A[8]=5, A[9]=6$; $A[5]=13 \ge A[10]=12$. Every parent is greater than or equal to its children, forming a valid max-heap.

questions.question_text:
Let SLLdel be a function that deletes a node in a singly-linked list given a pointer
to the node and a pointer to the head of the list. Similarly, let DLLdel be another
function that deletes a node in a doubly-linked list given a pointer to the node and
a pointer to the head of the list.
Let n denote the number of nodes in each of the linked lists. Which one of the
following choices is TRUE about the worst-case time complexity of SLLdel and
DLLdel?

options.A: SLLdel is O(1) and DLLdel is O(n)
options.B: Both SLLdel and DLLdel are O(log(n))
options.C: Both SLLdel and DLLdel are O(1)
options.D:
SLLdel is O(n) and DLLdel is O(1)
CS

questions.subtopic: Arrays, stacks, queues, linked lists
questions.explaination: In a singly-linked list, deleting a given node requires finding its predecessor node to bypass it, requiring an $\mathcal{O}(n)$ traversal from the head in the worst case. In a doubly-linked list, each node directly points to its predecessor (`node->prev`), allowing immediate pointer adjustments in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time.

questions.question_text:
The Lucas sequence Ln is deﬁned by the recurrence relation:
Ln = Ln−1 + Ln−2,
for
n ≥3,
with L1 = 1 and L2 = 3.
Which one of the options given is TRUE?
questions.subtopic: Combinatorics: counting, recurrence relations, generating functions
questions.explaination: The recurrence $L_n = L_{n-1} + L_{n-2}$ has characteristic equation $r^2 - r - 1 = 0$, giving roots $r_1, r_2 = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$. The general solution is $L_n = c_1 \left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^n + c_2 \left(\frac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^n$. Substituting initial conditions $L_1 = 1$ and $L_2 = 3$ yields $c_1 = 1$ and $c_2 = 1$.
questions.question_text_latex:
The Lucas sequence $L_n$ is defined by the recurrence relation:
\[ L_n = L_{n-1} + L_{n-2}, \quad \text{for } n \ge 3, \]
with $L_1 = 1$ and $L_2 = 3$.
Which one of the options given is TRUE?

questions.question_text:
Suppose two hosts are connected by a point-to-point link and they are conﬁgured
to use Stop-and-Wait protocol for reliable data transfer. Identify in which one of
the following scenarios, the utilization of the link is the lowest.

options.A: Longer link length and lower transmission rate
options.B: Longer link length and higher transmission rate
options.C: Shorter link length and lower transmission rate
options.D:
Shorter link length and higher transmission rate
CS

questions.subtopic: Transport layer: flow control and congestion control, UDP, TCP, sockets
questions.explaination: Link utilization in Stop-and-Wait is $\eta = \frac{1}{1 + 2a}$, where $a = \frac{T_{\text{prop}}}{T_{\text{trans}}} = \frac{d/v}{L/B} = \frac{d \cdot B}{v \cdot L}$. Utilization $\eta$ is lowest when parameter $a$ is maximized, which occurs when the link length $d$ is longer (increasing propagation delay) and the transmission rate $B$ is higher (decreasing packet transmission time).

options_latex.C: Shorter link length and lower transmission rate
options_latex.D: Shorter link length and higher transmission rate

questions.question_text:
CS

An algorithm has to store several keys generated by an adversary in a hash
table. The adversary is malicious who tries to maximize the number of collisions.
Let k be the number of keys, m be the number of slots in the hash table, and k > m.
Which one of the following is the best hashing strategy to counteract the adversary?

options.A: Division method, i.e., use the hash function h(k) = k mod m.
options.B:
Multiplication method, i.e., use the hash function h(k) = ⌊m(kA −⌊kA⌋)⌋, where
A is a carefully chosen constant.
options.D:
If k is a prime number, use Division method. Otherwise, use Multiplication method.
CS

questions.subtopic: Searching, sorting, hashing
questions.explaination: In universal hashing, the hash function is chosen uniformly at random from a carefully designed universal collection of hash functions independently of the keys. Because the adversary cannot predict which function will be selected at runtime, any fixed choice of malicious keys cannot guarantee worst-case collision behavior.
questions.question_text_latex:

Which one of the following is the best hashing strategy to counteract the adversary?

options_latex.B: Multiplication method, i.e., use the hash function $h(k) = \lfloor m(kA - \lfloor kA \rfloor)\rfloor$, where $A$ is a carefully chosen constant.

questions.question_text:
Which one or more of the following need to be saved on a context switch from one
thread (T1) of a process to another thread (T2) of the same process?
questions.subtopic: System calls, processes, threads, inter-process communication
questions.explaination: Threads of the same process share the process address space, open files, and the page table base register (PTBR is not switched). However, each thread has its own private thread control block (TCB) maintaining its program counter, stack pointer, and general purpose CPU registers, which must be saved during a thread context switch.

questions.question_text:
Which one or more of the following options guarantee that a computer system will
transition from user mode to kernel mode?
questions.subtopic: System calls, processes, threads, inter-process communication
questions.explaination: A transition to kernel mode is triggered by traps, exceptions, or hardware interrupts. A Page Fault is a hardware exception handled exclusively by the OS kernel (C is true). A System Call issues an explicit software trap instruction switching the CPU to kernel mode (D is true). Standard user-space function calls and `malloc` execute in user mode without inherently causing a mode transition.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?

options.A: The intersection of two regular languages is regular.
options.B: The intersection of two context-free languages is context-free.
options.C: The intersection of two recursive languages is recursive.
options.D:
The intersection of two recursively enumerable languages is recursively enumerable.
CS

questions.subtopic: Regular and context-free languages, pumping lemma
questions.explaination: Regular languages, recursive languages, and recursively enumerable languages are all closed under intersection (A, C, and D are CORRECT). Context-free languages are not closed under intersection; for example, $L_1 = \{a^n b^n c^m\}$ and $L_2 = \{a^m b^n c^n\}$ are both CFLs, but $L_1 \cap L_2 = \{a^n b^n c^n\}$ is not context-free.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT about
the OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) routing protocol used in the Internet?

options.A: OSPF implements Bellman-Ford algorithm to ﬁnd shortest paths.
options.B: OSPF uses Dijkstra’s shortest path algorithm to implement least-cost path routing.
options.C: OSPF is used as an inter-domain routing protocol.

questions.subtopic: Routing protocols: shortest path, flooding, distance vector and link state routing
questions.explaination: OSPF is an intra-domain (Interior Gateway) routing protocol that uses Dijkstra's link-state algorithm (not Bellman-Ford, which is used by distance-vector protocols like RIP). Therefore, statement A (implements Bellman-Ford) and statement C (used as inter-domain) are INCORRECT, which are the required answers.

questions.question_text:
Geetha has a conjecture about integers, which is of the form
∀x
P(x) =⇒∃yQ(x, y)
,
where P is a statement about integers, and Q is a statement about pairs of integers.
Which of the following (one or more) option(s) would imply Geetha’s conjecture?
questions.subtopic: Propositional and first order logic
questions.explaination: Geetha's conjecture states $\forall x [P(x) \implies \exists y Q(x, y)]$. Statement B ($\forall x \forall y Q(x, y)$) asserts $Q(x, y)$ holds for every pair, directly implying $\exists y Q(x, y)$ and therefore making the implication true for all $x$. Statement C ($\exists y \forall x [P(x) \implies Q(x, y)]$) provides a single $y$ that satisfies the implication for every $x$, which immediately implies that such a $y$ exists for each $x$.

Geetha has a conjecture about integers, which is of the form
\[ \forall x \, [P(x) \implies \exists y \, Q(x, y)], \]
where $P$ is a statement about integers, and $Q$ is a statement about pairs of integers. Which of the following (one or more) option(s) would imply Geetha's conjecture?

questions.question_text:
Which one or more of the following CPU scheduling algorithms can potentially
cause starvation?
questions.answer: A, C, D or C, D
questions.subtopic: CPU and I/O scheduling
questions.explaination: Priority Scheduling can cause starvation for low-priority processes if higher-priority processes arrive continuously (C). Shortest Job First (SJF) starves long burst jobs when short jobs arrive continuously (D). Under certain interpretations where FIFO queues suffer convoy effects or indefinitely waiting jobs in specific priority variants, FIFO was also credited, hence GATE accepted {C, D} or {A, C, D}. Round Robin provides bounded waiting and prevents starvation.

questions.question_text:
Let
f(x) = x3 + 15x2 −33x −36
be a real-valued function.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.A: f(x) does not have a local maximum.
options.C: f(x) does not have a local minimum.
options.D:
f(x) has a local minimum.
CS

questions.subtopic: Maxima and minima
questions.explaination: Setting $f'(x) = 3x^2 + 30x - 33 = 3(x+11)(x-1) = 0$ yields critical points $x = -11$ and $x = 1$. The second derivative is $f''(x) = 6x + 30$. Since $f''(-11) = -36 < 0$, $x = -11$ is a local maximum (B is TRUE). Since $f''(1) = 36 > 0$, $x = 1$ is a local minimum (D is TRUE).

Let f and g be functions of natural numbers given by f(n) = n and g(n) = n2.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.subtopic: Asymptotic worst case time and space complexity
questions.explaination: For $f(n) = n$ and $g(n) = n^2$, we evaluate $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{f(n)}{g(n)} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} = 0$. By definition, if the limit is 0, $f(n) \in o(g(n))$, which strictly implies $f(n) \in \mathcal{O}(g(n))$. Hence, both A and C are TRUE.

A particular number is written as 132 in radix-4 representation. The same number
in radix-5 representation is
.
CS
questions.subtopic: Number representations and computer arithmetic (fixed and floating point)
questions.explaination: Converting $132_4$ to base 10: $1 \times 4^2 + 3 \times 4^1 + 2 \times 4^0 = 16 + 12 + 2 = 30_{10}$. Converting $30_{10}$ to radix 5: $30 = 6 \times 5 + 0$, $6 = 1 \times 5 + 1$, $1 = 0 \times 5 + 1$. Reading remainders from bottom to top yields $110_5$.

questions.question_text:
Consider a 3-stage pipelined processor having a delay of 10 ns (nanoseconds),
20 ns, and 14 ns, for the ﬁrst, second, and the third stages, respectively. Assume
that there is no other delay and the processor does not suﬀer from any pipeline
hazards. Also assume that one instruction is fetched every cycle.
The total execution time for executing 100 instructions on this processor is
ns.
CS
questions.subtopic: Instruction pipelining, pipeline hazards
questions.explaination: The clock period of the pipeline is governed by the longest stage delay: $T = \max(10, 20, 14) = 20\text{ ns}$. For an ideal $k$-stage pipeline executing $n$ instructions, the total execution time is $(k + n - 1) \times T$. For $k = 3$ and $n = 100$: $(3 + 100 - 1) \times 20 = 102 \times 20 = 2040\text{ ns}$.

questions.question_text:
A keyboard connected to a computer is used at a rate of 1 keystroke per second.
The computer system polls the keyboard every 10 ms (milli seconds) to check for
a keystroke and consumes 100 μs (micro seconds) for each poll. If it is determined
after polling that a key has been pressed, the system consumes an additional 200
μs to process the keystroke. Let T1 denote the fraction of a second spent in polling
and processing a keystroke.
In an alternative implementation, the system uses interrupts instead of polling.
An interrupt is raised for every keystroke. It takes a total of 1 ms for servicing an
interrupt and processing a keystroke. Let T2 denote the fraction of a second spent
in servicing the interrupt and processing a keystroke.
The ratio T1
T2
is
. (Rounded oﬀto one decimal place)
CS
questions.subtopic: I/O interface: interrupt and DMA mode
questions.explaination: With polling every $10\text{ ms}$, there are 100 polls per second. Polling overhead is $100 \times 100\ \mu\text{s} = 10000\ \mu\text{s} = 10\text{ ms}$. With 1 keystroke/s, processing takes $200\ \mu\text{s} = 0.2\text{ ms}$, giving $T_1 = 10 + 0.2 = 10.2\text{ ms}$. In interrupt-driven mode, 1 interrupt per second takes $1\text{ ms}$, giving $T_2 = 1\text{ ms}$. The ratio is $\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{10.2}{1.0} = 10.2$.

questions.explaination: In `funcp()`, the static variable $x$ persists across invocations. On first call `x = funcp()`, static $x$ increments from 1 to 2 and returns 2, setting local $x = 2$. In `y = funcp() + x`, `funcp()` increments static $x$ from 2 to 3 and returns 3, so $y = 3 + 2 = 5$. Finally, `printf` prints $x + y = 2 + 5 = 7$.
